summary:
Echoes is an interactive web platform that lets students explore what NASA has found on Mars and the Moon, including discoveries from before they were even born. It uses real NASA data and images, and it’s simple enough that kids can start exploring with almost no instructions.

Along the way, each discovery is tied to ideas from Physics, Chemistry and Biology. A rover’s tools, the water ice on the Moon or the dust on Mars become a way into the science students already study in class, explained in a light and visual way. Many of these stories come from missions that have ended, like Opportunity, but whose findings still matter. That’s the idea behind the name: when a signal goes quiet, its echoes keep reaching us.

We’re building Echoes so schools, education networks and city governments can use it to bring quality science content to more students and support teachers in the classroom.
details:
Echoes: “Abandoned, but not forgotten.”

What it does and how it works

Echoes is a prototype of an interactive space museum that runs in the browser. It’s made for kids between 8 and 13, ideally explored with a teacher or another adult nearby, and we’re building it so schools and city education programs can use it too. We made it for the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: NASA’s Discarded Equipment Storytelling.”

The main story is about Opportunity, the Mars rover that was supposed to work for 90 days and ended up exploring Mars for more than 14 years. Visitors start in a 3D Solar System, pick a world, and scroll through the story. They see the original mission plan, a real NASA map of the rover’s final route, and an official 3D model they can poke at, including a “teardown” view where kids can look at the rover’s parts. Four short chapters tell what the mission was, what it found, and how it ended. We also show the real, incomplete image Opportunity sent back at the end, and then a short quiz and a final screen about what the rover left behind.

There’s a second journey on the Moon, with Apollo 11, the lunar exosphere, regolith, water ice and Artemis. And because not every school computer can handle 3D, we also made an Archive Mode: a plain, linear, text version that works without WebGL or animations.

Benefits

Most space content for kids ends up as a pile of facts. We wanted the images, maps and 3D models to work together as one story, so kids can see the evidence behind what they’re reading.

We also built it thinking about who actually gets to use it. It works with a keyboard, has captions, respects reduced-motion settings, offers optional narration, adapts to phones, and comes in Portuguese and English. Nothing essential depends on sound or 3D, and it runs in a browser with no installation, which matters for public-school computer labs. The story, the quiz and the Archive Mode also leave natural pauses where a teacher can stop and talk with the class.

Finally, you can always see where things come from. Every important image, model, map and fact shows its source, and we mark what is real NASA material and what is an artistic reconstruction. We chose not to present Opportunity’s last transmission as a “final message” or to invent a farewell for it.

Intended impact

We want kids to understand that a mission doesn’t stop mattering when its signal goes quiet. We’d like them to leave knowing not just what Opportunity did, but what it discovered and what it left for everyone.

Beyond that, we hope Echoes sparks interest in space and engineering, helps build the habit of looking at evidence, and makes NASA’s public archives feel closer to public-school students. For schools and city governments, we want it to be a low-cost, ready-to-use tool that supports teachers rather than replacing them. And since the format isn’t tied to one rover, it could be reused for other retired missions. Because Echoes is still a prototype, our next step is to test it in real classrooms.

Tools

We built it as a responsive web app with React 19, TypeScript, HTML and CSS, using Vite for builds. The 3D parts run on Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, animations use Motion, and Zustand handles the app’s state. We tested with Vitest, React Testing Library, Playwright and axe-core, and used the browser’s SpeechSynthesis for narration. The content comes from official NASA/JPL-Caltech resources: the Opportunity 3D model, the Mars texture, the final traverse map, mission photos and historical data. We also used Codex as an AI tool to help with development and quality checks.

How is the project creative?

An echo is what’s left after a sound stops. When Opportunity went silent, its echoes kept reaching us as discoveries and data that still shape how we understand Mars. That’s where the name comes from, and it’s the idea behind the whole project.

Instead of treating a retired rover as a list of facts, we treat it as a character with a journey, from a 90-day plan to more than 14 years on Mars. We tell the ending with the real incomplete image instead of an invented goodbye, because we think that honesty is part of the story.

What our team considered

We thought about who would use it: kids of 8 to 13, usually with an adult, in schools that may not have powerful computers. That’s why we focused on accessibility, a no-3D fallback and no installation. We also cared about scientific honesty, so we kept real and reconstructed material clearly separate, and about making the format easy to extend to other missions. We tested the code and accessibility as we went, and we were open about using AI tools.
